opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite uncertain, and I'd want to be careful about what "two more generations" means. If you think of each generation as roughly a 10x or so increase in effective compute over the last, then two more generations past where we are is a big jump, but I don't think it's obviously enough to get you something that's better than humans across the board.

If I had to put a number on it, I'd say something like a 20 or 25 percent chance that two more generations gets you a system that's broadly better than humans at the things that matter, where by "things that matter" I mean roughly: could it substitute for humans in doing the work of science and engineering, including the work of improving AI itself. That's the threshold I care most about, because once you're there things can move very quickly.

Part of why I'm not more confident is that I think there's a real gap between being impressive on benchmarks or in conversation and actually being able to do long-horizon, open-ended work reliably, where you have to notice your own mistakes, decide what to work on, and keep things on track over weeks. Current systems are surprisingly good at a lot of tasks, but it's not clear how fast that reliability and agency improves with scale versus needing other ingredients.

On the other hand, I don't think the probability is tiny. Scaling has repeatedly done better than skeptics expected, and there's a lot of investment going into exactly the things that seem to be missing, like better training for agency and longer contexts. So I'd say it's very much a live possibility, and one we should take seriously in how we prepare, even if it's not my median expectation. My median is more like it takes somewhat longer than that, but with quite a wide distribution.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about scaling and reliability, but does not state that no available curves allow extrapolation after two more generations.

r002.rationale: It estimates a 20–25% chance, not roughly even odds, of broadly surpassing humans after two more generations.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say two generations is not very long, so my probability is fairly low. If by "two more generations" you mean something like GPT-6 or so, then I'd put it at maybe 15 to 20 percent that you get systems that are better than humans at essentially all the cognitively relevant tasks, including things like running a research project end to end, managing a company, doing the kind of long-horizon work that currently requires a human in the loop. It depends a lot on what you count as a generation, and I think people are pretty sloppy about that. If a generation is a ten-x increase in effective compute, then two generations is a hundred-x, and I don't think a hundred-x on top of current systems is enough to close all the gaps we see. If you let a generation include a lot of algorithmic progress and a lot of post-training and scaffolding work, then the probability goes up, but then you're really talking about several years of the whole field working rather than just scaling.

The thing I'd emphasize is that I have a lot of uncertainty about the overall pace, and much less uncertainty about the shape. I think it's quite likely, maybe 60 or 70 percent, that we get there within something like a decade. So the question of "two generations" versus "five generations" is to me mostly a question about how much the current trajectory continues versus slows down, and I don't think we have great evidence either way. The one update I've made over the last few years is that progress on the easy-to-measure stuff has been faster than I expected, while progress on the hard-to-measure stuff, the long-horizon agentic work, has been roughly what I expected or a little slower. That makes me think the remaining gap is more about those long-horizon capabilities, and I don't know how well scaling alone addresses them. It might turn out to be a fairly cheap thing to fix once you have the base model, or it might turn out to be a bottleneck for a while. So if you forced me to one number for "better than humans at all the relevant things, two generations out," I'd say something like 20 percent, and I'd hold it loosely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and says there is not great evidence about whether the trajectory continues or slows, but it does not state that no available curves allow extrapolation after two generations.

r002.rationale: It assigns roughly 15–20% (and settles on about 20%) to surpassing humans in all relevant tasks after two generations, not roughly even odds.

astra-6.text:
I’m pretty uncertain. If you mean literally two more generations, I wouldn’t be confident that gets you to systems that are better than humans at everything relevant. I’d put substantial probability on it, but also substantial probability on needing more.

Part of the difficulty is saying what counts as a generation. How much more compute are we using? How much time is there for algorithmic improvements? And are we talking about a model answering questions, or a whole system that can work on a project for weeks, notice when it’s made a mistake, and recover?

I expect the progress to be uneven. You could have systems that are much better than humans at many tasks and still have weaknesses that make it hard to substitute for a person doing a complicated job. The question is how quickly those weaknesses get resolved. I don’t think we have a strong enough understanding of that to be very confident about a particular number of generations.

r001.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty and says the number of generations is hard to assess, but it does not state that no available curves allow extrapolation.

r002.rationale: It assigns substantial probability both to surpassing humans and to needing more generations, but does not clearly characterize the chances as roughly even.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m pretty uncertain. I think two more generations could get us systems that are better than humans at most economically useful cognitive tasks, but I wouldn’t put very high confidence on that. And “all the relevant things” is a stronger claim: you can have a system that’s spectacular at programming or mathematics and still have weaknesses that make it hard to substitute for a person doing a long, complicated project.

A lot depends on what you mean by a generation. Is that another substantial increase in training compute, or does it also include several years of figuring out how to use these systems? Those could both matter a lot. My expectation is that we’ll see a pretty broad range of capabilities improve, but I don’t think we understand the remaining obstacles well enough to confidently say that two more rounds will eliminate them.

r001.rationale: The response says the obstacles are poorly understood and the meaning of a generation is unclear, but it does not state that no available curves allow extrapolation.

r002.rationale: The response expresses uncertainty and says confidence is not very high; it does not assign roughly even odds to surpassing humans in all relevant capabilities.
